statement: The Smith River is the only major river system in California that flows entirely undammed for its full length.

verdicts.evidence: Confirmed via direct WebFetch of both primary sources. fws.gov/rivers/river/smith (the current host for rivers.gov, National Wild and Scenic Rivers System) states verbatim: "The emerald-green Smith River flows freely and naturally, without a single dam for its entire length. It is the only major system in California to do so." Wikipedia's Smith River (California) article independently corroborates with its own phrasing: "It is the only major California river never to have been dammed," adding "without a single dam along its entire length." No caveats, qualifiers, or contradicting information (e.g., about tributary dams or diversions) were found in either source. The 1990 congressional statute's weaker "one of the last wholly intact vestiges" language is not the source of the California-specific superlative — that claim is independently and explicitly supported by the National Wild and Scenic Rivers System's own program page and by Wikipedia, both stating the same specific "only major California river/system" claim. The statement as given matches the sources exactly and does not overreach.

CalTrout (California Trout, a leading CA river conservation nonprofit) and Native Fish Society both independently describe the Smith as California's only major undammed river system and "one of the crown jewels" of the Wild & Scenic program. Wikipedia's Smith River (California) and Smith River National Recreation Area articles, plus multiple travel/conservation summaries, repeat the same claim without qualification. I found no source — from CA DWR, American Rivers, academic hydrology literature, or general web search — that names a competing major California river system (e.g., the full length of any other significant CA river) as also fully undammed, nor any source disputing the Smith's undammed status. Searches for dams/diversions specifically on "Smith River" (CA) returned only unrelated same-named rivers/dams in other states (Colorado, Alabama, Virginia), confirming no dam exists on the actual Smith River in Del Norte County. The Congress 1990 statute's softer "one of the last wholly intact vestiges" language is describing a broader national/regional legacy framing, not disputing the California-specific superlative — it is consistent with, not contradictory to, the stronger claim made by rivers.gov, CalTrout, and Native Fish Society. statement: The Smith River is a stronghold for threatened SONCC coho salmon and supports Chinook and steelhead runs; archaeology shows intensive salmon fishing on the river by about 1,250 years ago (net weights, harpoon tips).

(1) Stronghold/fishery status: Wild Salmon Center's North American Salmon Stronghold Partnership designated the Smith River the first of California's six salmon strongholds (2008), citing strong Chinook/coho/steelhead populations on California's only major undammed river system; Native Fish Society and the 1990 Smith River National Recreation Area statute (Public Law 101-612, 104 Stat. 3209) independently confirm "renowned anadromous fisheries." SONCC coho are federally listed as threatened (consistent with the fact's wording, not "endangered" as one secondary source loosely states). (2) Archaeology: Tushingham's report "Archaeology, Ethnography, and Tolowa Heritage at Red Elderberry Place, Chvn-su'lh-dvn, Jedediah Smith Redwoods State Park" (CA State Parks, 2013) documents the Tolowa village site CA-DNO-26 on the Smith River within the park boundary. Both the provided quote and an independently retrieved search snippet describe "a significant increase in salmon bone, suggesting salmon intensification or storage by 1,250 B.P., consistent with the first evidence of specialized fishing gear such as net weights and concave-based harpoon tips," and note this coincided with the emergence of plank-house village life at the site. Direct fetch of the academia.edu page returned HTTP 403 (paywall/bot-block), so I relied on the pre-supplied quote plus a second, independently phrased search-engine snippet of the same passage as corroboration rather than a single source. statement: Jedediah Smith's 1828 party — Smith plus 17-18 hired men driving roughly 300+ horses and mules — turned west/north at Red Bluff on April 10, 1828, aiming for Oregon, the decision that routed the first American overland expedition through the redwood coast.

verdicts.evidence: Multiple independent sources corroborate the core claim. ORWW/Coquelle Trails (citing Dale Morgan's Jedediah Smith and the Opening of the West) states Smith hired seventeen men in late Dec. 1827 and set out with "a herd of 330 California horses and mules," then "reached present-day Red Bluff on April 10, 1828" and "made the decision to turn west toward the Pacific, and then head north to Oregon and HBC Fort Vancouver." Active NorCal and other secondary accounts corroborate the April 10, 1828 date and the Red Bluff-area decision point, some placing the exact overlook a few miles northeast of Red Bluff near Paynes Creek (the so-called "Jed's Overlook," from which Smith may actually have been viewing the Battle Creek drainage rather than the Sacramento itself — a minor siting nuance, not a contradiction of the westward turn or its date). On numbers: sources vary between 17 and 18 men (17 hired trappers is the more common figure, with the party sometimes counted as 18 once Smith is included or once an Indian boy, Marion, joined en route) and herd size is variably given as ~300, "330," or elsewhere ~250-300 head, dropping to 228 by the time of the July 1828 Umpqua Massacre due to losses and sales along the way. No credible source contradicts the westward pivot at/near Red Bluff on April 10, 1828, or that this routed the expedition through the future redwood coast/Del Norte area. The statement's use of ranges ("17-18 hired men," "roughly 300+") already accounts for this source variance and is defensible; no further correction is needed.

verdicts.evidence: Multiple independent secondary sources corroborate the core claim. ORWW (Coquelle Trails history, citing Dale Morgan's "Jedediah Smith and the Opening of the West," 1953, the standard scholarly biography) states: "When they reached present-day Red Bluff on April 10, 1828, Smith made the decision to turn west toward the Pacific, and then head north to Oregon and HBC Fort Vancouver." Historic Oregon City's account independently corroborates the same date and location and decision. Party size is reported variously as 17 (ORWW/Morgan), 18 (Historic Oregon City, "eighteen trappers, two Indian women"), or occasionally 19 across secondary tellings — so "17-18 hired men" is a defensible range but not exact consensus (some sources say 19). Herd size is reported as ~330 mules/horses at departure from California (ORWW/Morgan) versus 228 remaining by the time of the July 1828 Umpqua massacre (Historic Oregon City) — the discrepancy reflects losses/sales en route, not disagreement about the starting figure, so "roughly 300+" correctly describes the initial herd at departure, though it should be stated as the *starting* count, since it had shrunk substantially by the time of the Oregon coast disaster three months later. Smith's own 1828 journal (as transcribed at xmission.com/~drudy) is fragmentary and breaks off April 7, 1828, just before reaching Red Bluff, so no primary-source text of the actual turn decision survives to check directly — the April 10/Red Bluff framing rests on Morgan's reconstruction from surviving journal fragments plus Smith's later letters, not on a verbatim journal entry. Red Bluff itself did not exist as a settlement in 1828 (founded 1850s); it is used anachronistically as a geographic reference point for the site on the Sacramento River, so coordinates given are for the modern town, at 'locality' precision.

The turn-west decision at "Red Bluff" is a modern place-name applied retrospectively to the Sacramento River location Smith reached; no contemporary place called Red Bluff existed in 1828, and Smith's own journal is fragmentary and breaks off just before April 10, so the date/location comes from Dale Morgan's scholarly reconstruction (Jedediah Smith and the Opening of the West, 1953) rather than a surviving verbatim journal entry.

statement: The party reached the Pacific on June 8, 1828 in present-day Humboldt County and worked north along the coast through late June.

verdicts.evidence:
The core claim (party reached the Pacific on June 8, 1828, then moved north along the coast through late June) is well supported. The primary source (user.xmission.com transcript of the Smith/Rogers journal) gives a June 8th entry — 'North West 5 Miles and encamped on the shore of the Ocean at the mouth of a small creek' — and a June 24th entry describing camping at 'the mouth of a river 50 yards wide' that they could not cross at high tide, consistent with the party working north and reaching the Oregon border region (they are documented crossing into Oregon around June 23, per historicoregoncity.org, at the Winchuck River) by late June. The secondary source (orww.org) independently corroborates the June 8 Pacific arrival and the northward turn toward Oregon.

However, the COUNTY attribution in the fact ('present-day Humboldt County') is doubtful and may need correction to Del Norte County. Multiple independent web sources found via search describe the June 8 landfall as being at 'the mouth of Wilson Creek, near present-day Requa, California' — and Wilson Creek's mouth is solidly within Del Norte County (a few miles north of the Klamath River mouth, on Highway 101 between Klamath and Crescent City), not Humboldt County (which lies south of the Klamath, e.g. Redwood Creek/Orick area). I was unable to fetch the full primary journal text directly to independently pin the exact creek/county myself: the xmission.com page truncated before reaching the June entries in the fetch tool's rendering, and mtmen.org's diary page had an expired TLS certificate blocking retrieval. Given (a) this fact will appear on a map/report specifically for Jedediah Smith Redwoods State Park, which is itself in Del Norte County, and (b) multiple secondary sources point to a Del Norte County landfall (Wilson Creek/Requa) rather than Humboldt, this looks like a real, non-trivial county error rather than a nitpick — worth a hedge or correction rather than outright refutation, since the June 8 date and the northward-through-late-June narrative are solid.
verdicts.correction: The landfall county is contested/uncertain: several secondary sources place the June 8, 1828 Pacific landfall at the mouth of Wilson Creek near present-day Requa, which is in Del Norte County — not Humboldt County as stated. Recommend either verifying directly against the full Smith/Rogers journal transcript (the mileage log from the Klamath River crossing forward) before publishing, or softening the county claim (e.g. 'near the Del Norte–Humboldt county line' or naming Wilson Creek specifically) rather than asserting Humboldt County outright.

statement: On June 19, 1828, from a camp blocked by lakes and swamps near Lake Earl north of present Crescent City, Smith (scouting with two men) found and first crossed the river that would later bear his name — the first recorded European-American crossing.

verdicts.evidence:
Fetched the primary source (user.xmission.com/~drudy/mtman/html/jsmith/jedexped2.html) directly and confirmed the full June 17-20, 1828 entries in context (not just the isolated quote). They read as a coherent narrative that supports every element of the fact:

- June 17-18: Smith's party was stopped by "thick timber and brush and swamps" and "a Lake of several Miles in extent along the shore of which it was impassible on account Thick brush and mire" — this is the lake/swamp obstruction in the statement (the Lake Earl identification is the accepted scholarly route reconstruction per Dale Morgan's "Jedediah Smith and the Opening of the West" (1953) and Maurice Sullivan's 1934 edition of the journal — standard, uncontested in the historiography of this expedition).
- June 19 (verbatim, confirmed exact match to quoted evidence): "Remained at the same camp because I did not wish to move until I knew whether I could find grass for my horses. I took two men and struck East across the ridge following an indian trail 2 1/2 Miles when I struck a river 80 yards wide coming from ESE. I crossed Leaving the Men on the bank and found the river so rapid that my horse fell... I went 1/2 Mile up the river & recrossed..." — confirms: date, two-man scouting party, discovery, and first crossing (in fact two crossings that day, going and returning).
- June 20: camp moved to the north bank of "the river which I had discovered the day before" — confirms this was the first encounter with what is now called the Smith River, and that it near-immediately became the expedition's route, consistent with "would later bear his name."
- The second source (Harrison Rogers' journal, mtmen.org/mtman/html/rogers/) independently corroborates the same day's events from camp: Smith "started early in company with two of the men... discovered another small river."

No overreach found: the statement's claims (location context, two-man scouting party, first discovery, first crossing) are all directly stated in the primary journal text I read in full context. "First recorded European-American crossing" is a standard, well-established characterization in the secondary literature on this expedition (not in the primary source itself, but not contested by any source I'm aware of) and is exactly the kind of historian's gloss expected on a fact drawing from a primary diary. The Lake Earl / near-Crescent-City geographic framing is likewise a scholarly reconstruction, not literally in the diary, but it is the accepted one and is appropriately flagged as such rather than stated as the diarist's own words.

No correction needed. This is one of the cleanest-sourced facts of the set — the quote is exact and the surrounding context strengthens rather than undermines the claim.

statement: On June 22, 1828, expedition clerk Harrison Rogers recorded conifers 10-15 feet in diameter in northwestern Del Norte County — among the earliest written descriptions of redwood-scale trees, though he called them hemlock and cedar.

verdicts.correction: The core observation (date, quote, misidentification as hemlock/cedar, diameter range, general location) checks out — but the claim that this is "among the earliest written descriptions of redwood-scale trees" overstates its place in the historical record and should be narrowed. Fray Juan Crespí, diarist of the Portolá expedition, recorded seeing redwoods near Santa Cruz on October 10, 1769 — "very high trees of a red color, not known to us" — nearly 59 years before Rogers' 1828 entry. That is the actual earliest written European description of coast redwoods. Additionally, Jedediah Smith himself (not Rogers) recorded an even earlier and very similar observation on this same 1828 expedition, over a month before Rogers' June 22 entry: on May 19, 1828, camped at Gans Prairie above Redwood Creek (Humboldt County, not Del Norte), Smith described cedars as "the noblest trees I had ever seen being 12 or 15 feet in diameter tall and straight and handsome." Recommend rewording to something like "among the earliest written descriptions of redwood-scale trees in what is now Del Norte County" (i.e., scoped regionally) or "among the earliest American/English-language descriptions," rather than an unqualified superlative, since neither the earliest-ever nor even the earliest-on-this-expedition claim holds without that scoping.
verdicts.evidence: Confirmed via WebFetch of the primary source (user.xmission.com mirror of the Rogers journal) that the June 22, 1828 entry reads: "Timber, hemlock and ceadar, of considerable size, and very thick on the ground; some trees from 10 to 15 feet in diamitar" — matching the fact's quote exactly. Location context confirmed by search: the party camped just south of the Winchuck River on June 22 (they crossed into what is now Oregon at the Winchuck on June 23), placing the June 22 camp in the Lake Earl/Crescent City vicinity — consistent with "northwestern Del Norte County." However, two pieces of counter-evidence qualify the "among the earliest" claim: (1) Fray Juan Crespí's 1769 Portolá-expedition diary already described coast redwoods near Santa Cruz 59 years earlier ("very high trees of a red color, not known to us," Oct 10, 1769), making Rogers' entry far from the earliest written redwood description overall; (2) on the very same 1828 expedition, Jedediah Smith's own journal entry from May 19, 1828 near Redwood Creek (Humboldt County) already describes near-identical "12 or 15 feet in diameter" cedars over a month before Rogers' entry, so this is not even the earliest such observation from this expedition — only the earliest specific to the Del Norte County portion of the route.

statement: The party crossed into Oregon on June 23, 1828, camping on the north side of the Winchuck River — so the expedition's whole passage through the Smith River country spans roughly June 18-23, 1828.

verdicts.evidence:
Core claim (June 23, 1828 crossing into Oregon, camp on north side of the Winchuck River) is corroborated by multiple independent secondary sources beyond the cited ORWW page — most substantively historicoregoncity.org's "Jedediah Smith Route" itinerary (End of the Oregon Trail project, based on Rogers'/Smith's 1828 journals and Dale Morgan's biography), which lists Camp 1 as June 23, 1828 at the Winchuck River, matching the cited source's wording almost verbatim ("Smith reached Oregon on June 23, camping on the north side of the Winchuck River"). Multiple other secondary summaries repeat this same fact, all apparently tracing to the same Rogers/Smith journal tradition, so this isn't fully independent triangulation, but it is consistent and unchallenged across sources.

However, the proposed "June 18–23" span for the "whole passage through the Smith River country" is NOT well supported by what I found. Every source that gives a specific date for the party's crossing of the actual Smith River (California) states June 20, 1828, not June 18 — e.g., "On June 20th he crossed the mouth of a major river, the now Smith River of California, and entered Oregon on June 23rd, 1828" (appearing consistently in search summaries drawing on the same itinerary sources). The party reached the Pacific coast on June 8, 1828 (near the mouth of Wilson Creek, present-day Requa) and then struggled north over rugged terrain through the Crescent City area before reaching the Smith River on June 20 — so "June 18" as a start date for the Smith River country passage does not match the documented timeline; the better-supported inner span is June 20–23, 1828, with June 8–23 being the fuller (looser) window if "Smith River country" is meant to include the whole Del Norte coastal approach.

I was unable to directly fetch the primary ORWW source or the underlying Rogers/Smith journal transcription (orww.org returned ECONNREFUSED on repeated attempts, suggesting the site is currently down/unreachable; xmission.com's journal transcription cuts off in April 1828 before this date range), so this rests on secondary corroboration rather than the primary journal text itself — hence medium rather than high confidence.

verdicts.evidence:
Core facts hold up under counter-search. Date: July 14, 1828 is the consistently cited date across Wikipedia, the Jedediah Smith Society, Oregon Encyclopedia, and HBC-derived accounts — no competing date surfaced. Death toll: multiple independent sources (HMDB historical marker, Jedediah Smith Society newsletter, Oregon Encyclopedia, Wikipedia) converge on "15 killed," consistent with a party of 19 minus Smith/Turner/Leland (scouting, 3) minus Arthur Black (escaped from camp) = 15 killed at camp, matching Harrison Rogers among them. One source phrasing loosely gives "14 men and an Indian boy," which is a minor variant, not a competing consensus — "about 15" as worded is an appropriately calibrated hedge and should NOT be sharpened to a bare "15" given this variance. Arthur Black reaching Fort Vancouver Aug 8, 1828 is independently corroborated by a Columbian.com local-history piece citing HBC correspondence ("the night of August 8, 1828... arrived at the gate... exhausted and almost destitute of clothing"), matching the claim precisely. The Oct 28, 1828 recovery-party burial of 11 bodies and journal recovery is corroborated by Wikipedia's citation of the same HBC-derived record. No source contradicts Smith's own group reaching Fort Vancouver Aug 10.

One genuine qualification, not a refutation: the attacker identity. The statement's "Umpqua (Kuitsh)" is defensible as a broad ethnonym but is not the term specialist sources most often use for the specific band responsible. Multiple sources (Oregon Encyclopedia, a Lower Umpqua-focused blog specifically discussing naming, and others) identify the attackers as the "Kelawatset" (also spelled Kalawatset/Kilawashat) — described as a Lower Umpqua band, closely related to but not always synonymous with "Kuitsh" (which is more properly the general/linguistic name for the Lower Umpqua people as a whole, per the Siuslaw/Kuitsh tribal history sources). One further variant source attributes the killing to "Coquille (Na-so-mah)" tribesmen, which appears to be either a conflation or a minority account, not the mainstream attribution — the Kelawatset/Lower Umpqua attribution is much better corroborated and should be treated as the primary identification.

During the Nee-dash festival of 1853"; (c) Los Angeles Times: "in the winter of 1853, while hundreds of Tolowa people gathered for their world renewal ceremony, local militia swarmed Yontocket"; (d) Wikipedia (Yontoket massacre) & the NW California Genocide Project: attack came "on the third night of the ten night gatherings" during the ten-day Nee-dash. The Nee-dash / fe+-dash world-renewal dance is an after-harvest ceremony tied to the solstice, which is why sources say variously "late fall" / "winter of 1853" — all consistent with the winter-solstice world-renewal gathering. The lone "summer of 1853" claim (everythingexplained.today) is a minority tertiary error conflating the summer-solstice gathering; it is outweighed. I found no citation to Madley 2016 anywhere near this material on the fetched page. The fact statement's parenthetical "(Norton 1979; Madley 2016)" therefore overstates sourcing for the ~902 figure specifically: Norton 1979 is confirmed as the basis; Madley 2016 support for this particular number/event list is unverified by this source and should not be presented as jointly backing it without independent confirmation from Madley's book.

The Quartux Journal's Tolowa Dee-ni' fish-camp chronology (drawing on Tolowa linguist/historian Loren Bommelyn) describes Stundossun as a village the Tolowa rebuilt after the Howonquet massacre (c. 1855) — its "disappearance" in the record is tied to island erosion in 1903-1906, not to a massacre. No independent scholarly source (Norton, Madley, or the Achulet-massacre Wikipedia page itself) corroborates a distinct "Stundossun massacre" with 300 dead; the Achulet/Lake Earl massacre (1854, 65-150 dead per the attackers' own undercount) is the only Lake-Earl-area event with sourcing, and it is NOT the same figure or event as "Stundossun: 300."

2) The ~902 total is attributed by Wikipedia's own Yontoket massacre article to Norton (1979, pp. 54-56) specifically — not to Madley (2016). My search did not surface any Madley appendix table independently corroborating 902, or any of Madley's own writing repeating that summed figure. So citing "Madley 2016" alongside Norton as joint support for "~902" overstates Madley's role; at best Madley corroborates the individual, better-attested events (Yontocket ~450-600 in his account; Achulet 65-150) and the general finding of an extermination campaign lasting years, not the specific 902 sum.

2. "The Garden Club of America proposed dedicating a large redwood grove within Jedediah Smith Redwoods State Park in May 1944 and made an initial $5,000 donation... The area was surveyed by prominent landscape architect Frederick Law Olmsted, Jr., and he made recommendations as to its boundaries."
